definition: Branch-and-bound (BB, B&B, or BnB) is a method for solving optimization problems by breaking them down into smaller subproblems and using a bounding function to eliminate subproblems that cannot contain the optimal solution.
details: It is an algorithm design paradigm for discrete and combinatorial optimization problems, as well as mathematical optimization. A branch-and-bound algorithm consists of a systematic enumeration of candidate solutions by means of state-space search: the set of candidate solutions is thought of as forming a rooted tree with the full set at the root. The algorithm explores branches of this tree, which represent subsets of the solution set. Before enumerating the candidate solutions of a branch, the branch is checked against upper and lower estimated bounds on the optimal solution, and is discarded if it cannot produce a better solution than the best one found so far by the algorithm. The algorithm depends on efficient estimation of the lower and upper bounds of regions/branches of the search space. If no bounds are available, then the algorithm degenerates to an exhaustive search. The method was first proposed by Ailsa Land and Alison Doig whilst carrying out research at the London School of Economics sponsored by British Petroleum in 1960 for discrete programming, and has become the most commonly used tool for solving NP-hard optimization problems. The name "branch and bound" first occurred in the work of Little et al. on the traveling salesman problem.

explainer.lead: Branch and bound solves optimization problems by dividing the possible solutions into smaller groups and ruling out groups that cannot beat the best answer found so far. It can avoid checking every candidate, which matters for difficult problems with enormous numbers of possibilities.

tiers.eli5: Imagine searching many boxes for the best toy. If you can tell that everything in one box must be worse than a toy you already have, you can leave that box closed. Branch and bound keeps splitting the remaining boxes into smaller ones until it finds the best toy without opening every box.
tiers.practitioner: Represent the candidates as a rooted search tree, maintain the best solution found so far, and calculate bounds before enumerating a branch. For minimization, a branch whose lower bound cannot improve on the incumbent can be discarded; promising branches are subdivided and explored. Performance depends heavily on efficient, informative bounds: without bounds, the search becomes exhaustive.
tiers.paperLevel: For minimization over a candidate set S, represent subsets of S as nodes of a rooted tree and maintain an incumbent value z. At node v, estimate bounds for solutions in S_v; prune v when it cannot contain a solution better than z, otherwise partition S_v and continue the enumeration. Ailsa Land and Alison Doig proposed the method in 1960 for discrete programming, and the name “branch and bound” first appeared in work by Little et al. on the traveling salesman problem. Its effectiveness depends on bound estimation, and it degenerates to exhaustive search when no bounds are available.

explainer.example: Suppose a routing search has already found a complete tour of length 100. A partial route whose estimated lower bound is 108 can be discarded because completing it cannot beat 100, while a partial route with lower bound 92 must be split and explored further.

explainer.intuition: Instead of inspecting every possible answer, compare an entire group of answers with the best one already found. If the group cannot possibly contain anything better, discard the whole group at once.
howItWorks: Place the full set of candidate solutions at the root of a tree.
Split candidates into branches, with each branch representing a smaller subset.
Estimate upper and lower bounds for a branch before enumerating its candidates.
Discard the branch if those bounds show it cannot improve on the best solution found so far.
Otherwise, explore or subdivide the branch and update the best solution when a better one is found.
explainer.whyItMatters: Bounding can remove large parts of the search space while preserving the possibility of finding an optimal solution. This makes systematic search practical for many discrete and combinatorial problems where exhaustive enumeration would be much larger.
misconceptions: It is not simply exhaustive search with a different name, although it becomes exhaustive when no bounds are available.
It is not specific to the traveling salesman problem; it is a general paradigm for discrete, combinatorial, and mathematical optimization.
A branch is discarded because its bounds rule out an improvement, not merely because it looks unpromising.
